title: Distributed transactions: reaching one decision
lead: East must subtract four crates while West adds four. Each machine can protect and recover its own writes, but that alone cannot stop one machine committing while the other aborts. We will follow the messages and durable promises needed for one shared decision.
goals: Detect global deadlock by combining local graphs
Simulate prepare, vote, decision, and acknowledgement
Explain why a prepared participant can become blocked

sections.title: Local correctness leaves two global questions
sections.html:
Original example: East stores 12 crates and West stores 8 on separate machines. Transfer four: the desired final counts are 8 and 12, still totaling 20. Data is partitioned, meaning different machines hold different portions. For this lecture, there are no replicas. In the shared-nothing model, each machine has its own CPU, RAM and storage.

Each node can manage locks for its own records or pages. A table spanning nodes needs a designated authority for a table-level lock; granting a lock on one local fragment does not grant a lock on the whole logical table. A coordinator orchestrates a transaction, while participants perform its work on their local data.

First global question: can everyone get stuck despite each local graph looking safe?

NodeLocal waiting edgeLocal cycle?
EastT1 → T2No
WestT2 → T1No
Union of bothT1 → T2 → T1Yes

These arrows describe waiting for held locks, not the conflict order of completed operations. Combine local waits-for information and detect the global cycle, then choose and roll back a victim. Three nodes can hide the same issue with T1→T2, T2→T3, T3→T1.

Second global question: what if East commits the subtraction while West aborts the addition? Each local transaction could have valid logging and locking, yet only 16 crates remain. We need one decision for all participants. Remote communication can be delayed, reordered, or unavailable, so “tell everyone to commit” is not yet a failure-handling protocol. Nearby parallel systems and distant distributed systems differ in communication costs, but both must preserve the query's intended result.

Three machines report only T1→T2, T2→T3 and T3→T1 respectively. Why does checking each graph separately fail?

Worked answer. Each individual graph is a one-edge path, but their union requires T1 to wait around a closed loop. Detecting global deadlock requires global dependency information or an equivalent distributed detection method.

sections.title: A YES vote is a promise that must survive a restart
sections.html:
Coordinator C asks East E and West W whether they can finish the four-crate transfer. This is two-phase commit (2PC). The first phase gathers readiness; the second distributes the outcome. It differs from two-phase locking: 2PL orders data access, 2PC coordinates commit across nodes.

StepCoordinator CEast E / West W
1: prepareSends PREPARE to E and WCheck local work and ability to finish
2: voteCollects votesBefore YES, durably record PREPARE and needed recovery information; otherwise vote NO
3: decisionAll YES permits COMMIT; any NO means ABORT. Persist the decision before announcing itRemain prepared until the decision is known
4: finishSends the fixed decisionRecord/implement it, durably log completion as required, send ACK
5: bookkeepingCollect acknowledgements and record ENDDo not apply a duplicate message as a new transfer

“All YES” matters because a single participant may have insufficient stock, a constraint violation or another local failure. A majority cannot supply the missing crates. The prepared participant's YES is stronger than “I am currently willing”: after a crash it must still be able to obey the eventual outcome. Hence durable PREPARE precedes YES.

The coordinator likewise persists COMMIT before sending it. Otherwise E might receive COMMIT, C might crash and forget, then announce ABORT to W. Under the illustrated protocol, a participant persists its commit record before ACK so restarting cannot erase what its acknowledgement asserted.

END says the coordination work is finished; it is not a second opportunity to choose the outcome. Detailed slides show different logging conventions and optimizations, so do not infer a universal END-force rule. The central durable-before-message boundaries are the promises above.

Key takeaway

2PC coordinates commit; 2PL controls concurrent reads and writes. Two-phase commit protects atomic commit across machines. It does not replace an isolation protocol such as two-phase locking.

C has durable COMMIT, E acknowledged, but W’s ACK is lost. May C change to ABORT to stop waiting?

Worked answer. No. E may already have committed the subtraction. C must retain/resend the fixed COMMIT and process W’s eventual acknowledgement. The missing ACK means incomplete knowledge about completion, not an undecided outcome.

sections.title: Read recovery evidence according to each node’s role
sections.html:
Restarting nodes inspect durable records, not the last screen message. A node can coordinate one transaction and participate in another, so identify its role for this transaction first. The following recovery cases use the lecture's presumed-abort convention; its absence rules are part of that protocol, not universal laws about missing records.

Role and surviving recordsProtocol actionReason
Coordinator: COMMIT and ENDNo further commit-protocol workCompletion already recorded
Coordinator: COMMIT, no ENDRepeat phase 2Decision fixed; acknowledgements may be missing
Coordinator: ABORT / no transaction entry under this conventionUse ABORT response as specifiedPresumed-abort convention
Participant: no PREPAREMay abort locallyNo durable YES promise
Participant: PREPARE and COMMITComplete/acknowledge COMMITOutcome known
Participant: PREPARE onlyAsk coordinator; possibly waitOutcome not locally known
Participant: ABORTFinish according to abort conventionLocal undo/cleanup still matters

“No protocol work” does not mean “skip local recovery.” Data pages may still need redo/undo according to the outcome. A PREPARE-only participant must not be treated as an ordinary uncommitted single-node loser. Another participant might already have committed.

Message retransmission also needs state. If W committed the addition but its ACK was lost, repeating COMMIT should lead to another acknowledgement, not another +4. Transaction IDs and remembered state distinguish the same decision from a new transfer.

The lecture orders messages densely within each sender/receiver/transaction-ID stream: 1,2,3,… . If k+1 arrives while k is missing, buffer k+1 until its predecessor is resolved. A message from another stream cannot fill that gap. Numbering detects gaps and duplicates; it does not make lost messages arrive.

A participant restarts with only PREPARE. The coordinator restarts with COMMIT but no END. What should happen?

Worked answer. The participant inquires; the coordinator retains COMMIT and repeats phase 2. The participant completes that decision and acknowledges it. Local absence of COMMIT was uncertainty, not permission to abort.

sections.title: Two remote histories look identical to a waiting participant
sections.html:
E has durably prepared and sent YES. It times out waiting for C. Consider two possible remote histories:

What E can seeRemote history ARemote history B
Its own logPREPARE onlyPREPARE only
Coordinator and WC has not decided; W might vote NOC logged COMMIT; W received it and committed
Message to ENo decision has arrivedCOMMIT was delayed or lost

E's local evidence is identical in both. If E guesses COMMIT, it can violate history A where W must abort. If it guesses ABORT, it violates history B where W has already committed. A timeout establishes only that a message has not arrived within a chosen interval; it does not establish the global outcome or even prove C has failed.

E must obtain an authorized decision from C or a participant that can establish it under the protocol. Without sufficient information it remains in doubt and may block. This sacrifices availability to preserve atomicity; it is not a claim that every failed node stops every transaction.

The cost spreads through locks. Under the lecture's strict 2PL convention, E still holds its S/X locks while prepared. A new transaction wanting the same item waits too. Releasing protection or undoing locally to improve responsiveness would expose a state inconsistent with a remote commit.

The basic failure-handling argument assumes recovery evidence survives and nodes eventually return. If communication or a coordinator remains unavailable indefinitely, that assumption cannot give a finite completion time.

Key takeaway

A timeout does not prove that the transaction aborted. Another machine may already have committed while its notification was lost. A prepared participant cannot independently abort merely to stop waiting.

Does YES permit E to commit independently when C is unreachable? Does the timeout permit independent abort?

Worked answer. Neither. YES is readiness, and W may still have voted NO; timeout is missing information, and W may already have committed. E needs the permitted common outcome or must wait.

sections.title: Put the lock timeline beside the message timeline
sections.html:
Try the original transfer with a second reader T2. T1 has changed E from 12 to 8 and W from 8 to 12, both uncommitted. It holds the needed X locks. E and W prepare; E sends YES. Before E receives a decision, T2 asks to read E's count.

EventT1 commit state at ELock consequence
Writes finished locallyActive, no shared outcomeX lock still held
PREPARE durable / YES sentPrepared and in doubtX lock still held; T2 waits
COMMIT received and made durableKnown outcome; complete local commitRelease at completion; T2 can read 8
Alternatively, ABORT resolvedUndo E from 8 to 12Release after undo; T2 can read 12

Do not release at YES: readiness is not completion. With densely ordered per-transaction messages, a participant processes the commit request after earlier work in that stream and has its required locks. Apply the final decision and release protection consistently, so another transaction cannot observe a half-completed local outcome.

Optional: replicated decisions are a different layer

The lecture mentions three-phase commit and Paxos Commit as extensions; it does not teach their complete algorithms. Adding replicas alone does not specify who can decide, what survives a failure, or when progress is possible. A protocol must define agreement and failure assumptions.

Suppose East and West are transaction participants, while three other machines replicate decision information. Two of those three may form a decision-replica quorum. That quorum is not a majority vote replacing participant readiness: West's NO still prevents COMMIT. Agreement replicas record the correct transaction outcome; they cannot make West's failed constraint valid.

Keep the two jobs separate when reading a design: 2PL controls conflicting access and retains protection through uncertainty; 2PC coordinates atomic completion. Replication/consensus, when used, needs its own safety and progress argument.

T2 proposes reading E immediately after its YES and treating the count as committed because two decision replicas agree. What is missing?

Worked answer. E is still prepared and holds a conflicting lock; readiness does not settle the global outcome. A replica majority does not replace every participant’s readiness or the fixed decision. T2 waits until T1 resolves and completes, then reads the committed or restored count.

quiz.question: A participant has only a durable PREPARE record and loses contact with the coordinator. What is safe?
options: Commit independently because it voted YES
Abort immediately when a timeout expires
Seek the decision; it may have to wait
Delete the log and start over
quiz.explanation: A YES vote is a promise to follow the common decision. The coordinator may already have committed elsewhere.

source.summary: Lecture 22 studies partitioned, nonreplicated data, distributed locking, global deadlock, two-phase commit, and the coordination of logging with recovery. Two-phase commit can block progress when the coordinator is unreachable.

limitations: The lecture assumes partitioning without replication. Consensus-based improvements are mentioned but not developed in detail.
